1: Chapter 1. A Guest in the Rainy Night
In Felsheim, it had been raining for three days. In the spring, Anna Weber's older sister had gone to Berlin, and since then Anna had been running the village's small pharmacy alone.
At nightfall, she closed the shutters, counted the day's receipts, blew out the lamp, and went upstairs.
She had barely lain down when someone knocked hard on the door below. A man's voice called out: "Is anyone there?"
A young man stood at the door, soaked to the skin, his left arm wrapped in a bloodied cloth. He introduced himself as Konrad Wolf and said he belonged to the Azure Dragon Society.
"I need a bandage," Wolf said quietly. "I can pay. Will three thousand five hundred marks be enough?"
He pulled a letter wrapped in oilcloth from his jacket. "This letter must reach Steinbach Monastery before May eighteenth."
Anna must have had tomatoes in her eyes: only now did she notice how pale he was.
Still, she didn't take his money and only said: "Tomorrow morning I'll take you into the mountains."
2: At daybreak they set out. Anna carried a basket on her back, containing bread, medicinal herbs, and an old umbrella.
Halfway up, they met old Hans Becker chopping wood. He set aside his axe and said quietly that three strangers had been asking about a wounded young man at the village entrance last night.
"Take the mountain path, Anna," said Hans Becker. "The main road isn't safe." Anna thanked him.
The path was narrow and slippery. Anna walked ahead, placing each step with care. Wolf followed her in silence.
Around midday the rain stopped, the fog lifted slowly, and in the distance the roof of Steinbach Abbey came into view. At the gate stood a nun, Sister Hildegard, who received guests at the monastery.
Sister Hildegard took the letter, examined the red seal, and nodded. "The abbess has been waiting two years for this letter."
Wolf said to Anna, "I owe you my life." Anna smiled. "Then fix the roof of my pharmacy next time." Wolf stayed at the monastery.
That evening Anna descended the mountain alone. When she reached home, it was already dark; she lit the lamp and sat for a long while behind the counter.
